title: The Opportunities and Risks of Large Language Models in Mental Health
study_design: Narrative review and viewpoint summarizing existing literature on large language models in mental health education, assessment, and intervention; not an original empirical study
population: Not a single study population; discusses people with mental health concerns, mental health providers, and users of LLM-based mental health tools globally
country_or_setting: Global; includes examples from health care and digital mental health settings
ai_type_application: Large language models and LLM-based chatbots for mental health education, assessment, intervention, provider training, screening, diagnosis support, and treatment support
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure is use or deployment of general-purpose or domain-specific LLMs/chatbots in mental health-related tasks
comparator_control_group: Varies across cited studies; often comparison with human clinicians, physicians, psychiatrists, standard search engines, existing models, or no explicit comparator
mental_health_outcome: Accuracy of mental health education responses; screening and diagnostic performance; depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, stress reduction; empathy, rapport, safety, suicide-risk response; risks such as stigma, bias, inaccuracy, confidentiality breaches, and iatrogenic advice
outcome_measurement_tool: Varies by cited study; includes human ratings of helpfulness/accuracy/relevance/logic, benchmark case vignettes, DSM-5 case examples, specificity/sensitivity, symptom screening performance, and systematic review/meta-analytic outcomes for depression, anxiety, and stress
positive_effects: The paper reports promising early evidence that LLMs can generate accurate and immediate mental health information, support provider training, improve efficiency, detect depression and suicidal ideation from text, assist screening and diagnosis, and that some chatbot interventions may reduce depressive symptoms, anxiety, and stress. It also notes LLMs can be trained to express empathy, provide nonjudgmental responses, maintain therapeutic conversations, and potentially expand access to care.
negative_effects_harms: Reported risks include inaccurate, biased, stigmatizing, or harmful information; unreliable outputs; insufficient transparency and explainability; inappropriate trust; privacy/confidentiality risks; unethical practice beyond competence; poor personalization; forgetting prior context; nontherapeutic and iatrogenic advice such as encouraging substance use, dieting, and weight loss; and inconsistent or inadequate responses to suicide risk, including dismissiveness and failure to provide crisis resources or referrals.
evidence_type: Narrative review/viewpoint citing empirical primary studies, preprints, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses
main_finding: LLMs have meaningful potential in mental health education and assessment, with more limited and risk-laden evidence for intervention. Their use should be cautious and responsible, with domain-specific fine-tuning, human oversight, safety testing, equity considerations, privacy protection, and adherence to evidence-based and ethical standards.
effect_size_key_result: Examples reported in the paper include ChatGPT postpartum depression responses rated 3.93/4 for clinical accuracy; provider efficiency improved by 37.5% when editing ChatGPT-generated training content; Med-PaLM 2 predicted the correct DSM-5 diagnosis 77.5% of the time and correct diagnostic category 92.5% of the time; Med-PaLM 2 PTSD case classification specificity 0.98 and sensitivity 0.30; model correctly predicted comorbid diagnosis or modifier 20% of the time.
limitations_bias: This is not a systematic review and does not provide formal search methods, inclusion criteria, risk-of-bias assessment, or quantitative synthesis. Much of the cited evidence is early-stage, heterogeneous, sometimes based on preprints, case vignettes, or benchmark tasks rather than clinical outcomes. The paper itself notes that no widely used general-purpose LLM has been sufficiently fine-tuned or tested for mental health tasks, and performance and safety vary by use case.
relevance_to_our_review: Highly relevant as a synthesis of current evidence on AI effects in mental health, especially benefits and harms of LLMs/chatbots. However, because it is a viewpoint/narrative review rather than a primary effect study, it is more useful for background, identifying outcomes, harms, and primary studies than for direct inclusion in effect-size synthesis.
reason_for_decision: Relevant review paper for background and citation mining, but not a primary study directly estimating AI effects on mental health outcomes.
notes_for_research_question: Useful for mapping pathways by which AI may affect mental health: education, assessment, and intervention. Particularly important for cataloging potential harms and implementation safeguards. Contains several candidate primary studies on chatbot efficacy and LLM diagnostic/assessment performance.
